label: The News and Fear
framing: The news is built to keep you afraid, because fear holds attention and attention is the product being sold. Scripture does not tell you to ignore the world's pain but it tells you again and again, do not be afraid, and it anchors your peace in a God who is not surprised by the headlines.
cultural: We drink a steady stream of catastrophe from every corner of the earth, more than any human heart was built to carry, and we mistake the constant intake for being informed. The result is not wisdom but a low dread, a sense that everything is collapsing, an outrage that exhausts and never acts. Most of us have scrolled the worst of the world before breakfast and called it staying aware.
historical: Every generation has believed it stood at the end of the world, and the early church lived under an empire that fed Christians to beasts, yet Jesus told his followers not to let their hearts be troubled. Augustine answered the sack of Rome in 410 with the City of God, refusing panic, distinguishing the city of man that rises and falls from the city of God that endures. The sky has been falling for a long time, and the church has kept singing.
application: Set limits on your intake, choosing a time and a source rather than a constant drip, and refuse to let the headlines be the first and last thing your mind touches each day. Turn what you cannot control into prayer and what you can into action, however small and local. Stay informed enough to love your neighbor, and protected enough to keep your peace. The world is in better hands than the news will ever admit.

verses.text: God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble. Therefore we will not fear, though the earth is transformed and the mountains are toppled into the depths of the seas, though their waters roar and foam and the mountains quake in the surge.
verses.where: The psalm says God is our refuge and strength, so we will not fear though the earth gives way and the mountains fall into the sea. The site's plain note says it does not tell you not to fear because nothing bad will happen; it tells you not to fear because of who is with you when it does. The psalm puts God next to the trouble without making the trouble small.

verses.text: “Do not call conspiracy everything these people regard as conspiracy. Do not fear what they fear; do not live in dread. The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.
verses.where: As Assyria threatens and the people of Judah panic, God tells Isaiah not to call conspiracy everything the people call conspiracy, and not to fear what they fear: the LORD of Hosts is the one to regard as holy and to fear. The site's note on the chapter says Isaiah is told to fear the Lord, who will be a sanctuary for some. A people's shared dread is not a reliable guide to what is true.

verses.text: At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. To this He replied, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this fate? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.
verses.where: Some in the crowd bring Jesus the news of Galileans killed by Pilate. The site's note says Jesus names the assumption behind the report before anyone voices it, that the victims must have been worse sinners, and denies it flatly. The plain note says he turns the question from what the dead had done to where the living stand with God. It shows how to hear bad news: without blaming the victims, and without imagining we are safer than they were.

verses.text: I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!”
verses.where: On the night before his death Jesus tells his disciples that in the world they will have tribulation, but to take courage, because he has overcome the world. The site's plain note says he does not deny the trouble; he says it does not have the last word. The victory is real now, and it is not yet complete.

verses.text: The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him.
verses.where: The proverb observes that the first to state his case seems right until another comes and examines him. The site's note on the chapter gathers its sayings on hasty answers and lawsuits. A first report, however confident, is not yet the whole story, and wisdom waits for the other side.

verses.text: Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper.”
verses.where: Jeremiah writes to exiles in Babylon in 597 BC, telling them to build houses, plant gardens, raise families and pray for the welfare of the city where they live. The site's note says he warned against prophets promising a quick return. In a world that was not theirs and was not getting better on their schedule, God's people were told to seek its good.

verses.text: During the night, the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and he blessed the God of heaven and declared: “Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to Him. He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to the discerning.
verses.where: Facing a king's order to kill all the wise men, Daniel and his friends pray, and when God reveals the mystery Daniel blesses him: he changes times and seasons, removes kings and establishes them. The site's note tells how the dream ended in a stone that became a mountain filling the earth. Rulers rise and fall in every age; the one who sets them up does not.

verses.text: Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain? The kings of the earth take their stand and the rulers gather together, against the LORD and against His Anointed One: “Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords.” The One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord taunts them.
verses.where: The psalm asks why the nations rage and the rulers plot, and answers that the One enthroned in heaven laughs. The site's note says the contrast in posture is the argument: the rebels stand, God sits. The plain note adds that the first Christians prayed this psalm not for revenge, but for courage.

verses.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.
verses.where: Among Paul's short commands about sincere love is this one: rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep. The news brings a stream of other people's sorrow. Scripture's answer is neither to look away nor to be swallowed by dread, but to weep with real people and pray for them.

verses.text: Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls, yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!
verses.where: Habakkuk, trembling at what is coming, says that though the fig tree does not bud and the fields produce no food, yet he will rejoice in the God of his salvation. The site's note says he resolves to wait quietly for the day of distress. His joy did not depend on the headlines of his own day.

links.label: Practical guides for life in the world

misread.taken: Wars and rumors of wars are read in the news as proof that the end is about to come, so that every new war, earthquake or crisis is treated as a countdown and a reason for fear.
misread.says: The site's plain note says every age has had wars, earthquakes and famines, and in every age someone has said they prove the end is here. Jesus says the opposite: these things must happen, but the end is still to come. They are not a countdown; they are the normal weather of a broken world, and Jesus tells his followers not to be alarmed. The note adds that the first danger Jesus names is not war but being fooled, and asks who we let tell us what the news means.
misread.text: When you hear of wars and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things must happen, but the end is still to come.

whole: For many people bad news now arrives all day long. A war on the other side of the world, a shooting, a storm, an election, a scandal, a market falling: it arrives on the phone before breakfast and follows them to bed. Some of it is close and real; much of it is far away and out of their hands. They feel they ought to know, and they feel worse for knowing. Some find themselves anxious, some angry, some numb, and many sure that everything is falling apart and that the other side is to blame. The feeling of dread can grow quite apart from anything in their own street or week.

Scripture knew rumors and panic long before screens. Isaiah's neighbors saw conspiracy everywhere as Assyria marched, and God told him not to fear what they feared. A crowd brought Jesus the news of Galileans killed by Pilate and assumed the victims must have deserved it. Jesus warned that people would point to every war and earthquake as a sign, and that the first danger was being fooled. Our own fear often has a shape the Bible recognizes: we let the loudest voice tell us what is happening and what it means, we look for someone to blame so that we can feel safer, and we treat the news as if it decided everything. That temptation runs in every direction, through every party and every church, and it runs through us.

So the Bible's wisdom is to fear God and not the crowd, and to love the people the news is about. Listen to the second witness before you decide, as Proverbs says. Refuse to blame the victims of disaster, as Jesus refused. Weep with those who weep and pray for them by name. Seek the good of the place where you live, as the exiles in Babylon were told to do, rather than only fearing what may become of it. It may mean choosing when and how much news to take in, and putting the phone down before sleep. It means turning from what the headlines say to who God is, the one who changes times and seasons and sets up rulers and removes them.

The hope Scripture gives is that history is not running loose. God is our refuge and strength, an ever-present help in times of trouble, and the One enthroned in heaven is not anxious. In the world there will be tribulation, Jesus said, but take courage: he has overcome the world. The kingdom Daniel saw grows like a stone into a mountain, slowly and surely, while kingdoms rise and fall around it. Bad news will keep coming until he comes. It does not get to decide who we are, or what we hope in.
deep.sit: Who or what has been telling you what the news means, and what would change if you prayed for the people in the next headline instead of only fearing it?

prayer.lead: The end of the psalm of the toppling mountains, where God's own voice says be still and know that I am God. The site's plain note on the psalm says it does not make the trouble small; it puts God next to it.
prayer.text: Come, see the works of the LORD, who brings devastation upon the earth. He makes wars to cease throughout the earth; He breaks the bow and shatters the spear; He burns the shields in the fire. “Be still and know that I am God; I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted over the earth.” The LORD of Hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress.
